mutants.non_obvious_insight: The party with the most to lose from a stuck case is the employer, yet employers have never been the buyer because immigration law treats the individual as the client; third-party payer rules allow the employer to pay while the worker stays the client. Once the employer pays, the product changes character: expiry dates are known a year ahead, so demand is a forecastable renewal calendar and recurring subscription instead of lumpy, panicked legal purchases. And the employer's I-9 tickler is already the distribution asset, since it holds exactly the dates that trigger the suit.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-7: build the calculator as a spreadsheet plus web form and run it on anonymized expiry lists from 3 friendly employers. Days 1-10: sign 2-3 panel attorneys admitted in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y. and D.N.J. at $1,750 flat and get an employment-law read on third-party-payer, anti-discrimination and prepaid-legal-plan rules. Days 7-30: contact about 60 NYC-metro and NJ home-care agencies and staffing firms through state association events and LinkedIn, lead with their own calculator output, and close 3 paid pilots at about $2,500/month concierge plus per-case fees. Go/no-go: at least one employer with a real expiring cohort authorizes a filing within 30 days, and outcomes are logged to seed the ledger.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Mandamus.com sells single suits to individuals at $5,000 with SEO funnels and cannot run a workforce calendar for an employer. I-9/E-Verify vendors track expiry dates but stop at an alert (not verified in this research); they are channel partners, not rivals. Docketwise and Boundless serve firms and individuals on petitions, not employer-paid remedies. Alma sells O-1/EB-1 strategy to companies for high-skill hires, not frontline EAD renewals. Large corporate immigration firms serve professionals where ticket sizes are big; a $1,750 frontline case is below their radar (unverified). DoNotPay and free pro se guides cannot give an employer a managed, attorney-signed service with status reporting. Employer ownership of the buyer relationship is the wedge none of them hold.

mutants.title: Solos Refer, We File: National Delay-Suit Bench
mutants.one_liner: Invert the tool model: a lawyer-owned litigation bench that takes stuck cases referred by immigration solos, files at industrial speed for about 60% of the boutique price, and pays the referring lawyer a fee share, building a national referral network and the full-cycle dataset as a by-product.
mutants.customer: Payer: stuck applicants (post-interview N-400, I-751, I-765, long-idle I-130/I-140) referred by their own immigration lawyer, paying a $2,995 flat fee plus about $455 in costs. Channel: 1-10 attorney immigration firms in NY, NJ and CT that hold stuck clients but will not be counsel of record on a federal suit. Expansion: solos in any state, then boutique firms as overflow customers.
mutants.problem: The parent's model needs solos to pay $400 to do something they fear, and the research found no evidence that solos pay for tooling. What solos do have is client trust and a pile of stuck files. Their current choices are to do nothing or to refer the client to a boutique for no reward and the risk of losing the client. Meanwhile the one visible provider (Mandamus.com) is a small boutique with about 30 litigated petitions in 15 years, prices at $5,000 plus $500, and runs no co-counsel program for other lawyers. That leaves a large pool of unserved clients who cannot pay $5,000.
mutants.solution: A lawyer-owned litigation bench with the software company as management-services provider under a flat per-case fee (not a percentage of legal fees). The referral flow: a solo submits a stuck case through a 4-minute referral link or a case-management export; the ledger triages it (declining nationality-hold suits and Fifth Circuit I-485 claims); the client e-signs a fee-division consent that names each lawyer's share and the joint responsibility; the bench files within 72 hours, runs the 60-day clock, negotiates consent-order-first, and files the EAJA petition when a consent order supports it. The referring lawyer stays counsel on the underlying application, receives status in their own system, and earns 30% ($900) of the fee. The flat fee covers all litigation including an MTD opposition, matching the boutique's promise. Key legal gate: joint-responsibility fee division rules vary by state (NY 1.5(g) and ABA Model Rule 1.5(e) style), so launch only where ethics counsel clears it.
mutants.why_now: AI drafting and docket automation cut attorney time per routine filing from 6-10 hours to about 3 with paralegal support, which lets price fall to roughly 60% of the boutique at a healthy margin. The USAO's 45-90 day resolution pattern means one litigator can carry 60-100 live files, so the constraint on a litigation shop is intake, not lawyer time. Solos are overloaded and fear being first to file. The research found no co-counsel or referral program for other lawyers, so the economics of referral are unexploited.
mutants.revenue_model: Client pays $2,995 flat (court costs about $455 passed through). Referral share $900. Illustrative unit economics (assumptions): about $300 paralegal and attorney time, $40 service, about $225 expected tail (15% of cases x roughly $1,500 of MTD opposition work), $60 support, leaving about $1,450 contribution per case. 3,000 cases a year (a year-3 target that requires expanding the market, since the RECAP sample shows only 350-480 filings a year) would produce about $4.3M contribution. Upside: license the ledger, sell overflow capacity to boutiques, and reuse the same referral rails for other agency-delay claims (consular administrative processing, FOIA, passports).
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not tooling but willingness to be counsel of record. Solos already own client trust and stuck files but earn nothing from referring out and fear the suit; a fee share for zero litigation risk turns them from prospects who must be persuaded to pay into an eager, unpaid-acquisition channel, at 30% of fee versus the boutique's SEO and ad spend. Because most cases moot in weeks, the bench recycles capacity fast, and it is the bench, not a tool, that naturally accumulates the full-cycle data (service date, USCIS action date, fee outcome) that makes the ledger better than anyone's public docket analytics. Scale economies and a referral network are both reachable within 24 months.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: get an ethics-counsel memo for NY, NJ and CT on joint-responsibility fee division and a flat-fee MSO; secure a lawyer cofounder or contract litigator admitted in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y., D.N.J. and D. Conn. (the Mandamus.com boutique, admitted in D. Conn., D.D.C. and S.D. Tex., is a possible bench partner rather than only a rival); draft the referral agreement and client consent. Days 10-30: recruit 15 NY/NJ/CT solos through AILA chapters and direct outreach to attorneys of record on RECAP naturalization suits, pre-load 30 stuck cases from their own books, file the first 10 within 72 hours of consent, log every outcome, and pay the first referral share when the client pays. Go/no-go: 10 cases filed, more than half of referrers sending a second case, and modeled contribution of at least $1,000 per case.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Mandamus.com is a capacity-limited boutique acquiring clients by SEO at $5,000 and shows no co-counsel program; this acquires clients through lawyers who already hold them, prices at about 60% of the boutique, and can even contract the boutique's attorney as bench capacity. Docketwise has no litigation feature and is the natural place for a 'refer this case' button, so it is a channel, not a rival. Alma and Boundless have stuck clients and no litigation offer, so they are referral sources. Lex Machina, Trellis and CourtListener sell analytics or raw data, not filing capacity. DoNotPay and free pro se guides push risk onto the applicant; this puts a signed federal litigator behind every filing. Selective intake (no nationality-hold or Fifth Circuit I-485 cases) protects the win rate that competitors' broad templates cannot.

mutants.title: Serial Match: AP-Only Recovery for Exchange Buyers
mutants.one_liner: A success-fee audit that takes one accounts-payable export from an independent rotable pool or Part 145 station, finds money its repair vendors already owe, and collects it. It starts with credits the vendor has already conceded, then moves to repeat-failure claims.
mutants.customer: Independent rotable exchange pools, parts resellers and Part 145 stations that buy a few hundred outsourced repairs and exchange units a year from 10 or more shops, roughly $5-40M of repair spend (my assumption, unverified). The buyer is the Controller or VP Materials at a firm with a 2-4 person back office. These firms sit outside power-by-the-hour contracts, so the warranty exposure is theirs. They multi-source on price, so they have little vendor-relationship fear. They also see the same serial number pass through many hands. Regionals, EMS operators and lessors are phase 2.
mutants.problem: The parent idea had four named weaknesses: PBH and maintenance-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets, integrating with each operator's maintenance system is hard, fear of annoying the shop, and no proof anyone pays. A pool has none of these. Its serialized units cycle through repair invoices, exchange credits and core returns. The same P/N and S/N can appear on two invoices from one shop within the warranty window, and nobody joins invoice lines by serial number. Beside that sit credit memos issued but never applied, core credits not netted, no-fault-found evaluation fees on in-warranty units, and turnaround guarantees never credited. Pool gross margins are thin, so recovering 1-3% of repair spend moves EBITDA. The warranty windows are short and full of exclusions, so recovery has to be systematic, with a claim filed for every eligible unit.
mutants.solution: Input is one vendor-ledger export plus the invoice PDFs, with no maintenance-system integration. An LLM extractor builds a serial-level table: P/N (including interchangeable P/Ns), S/N, repair date, charges and the warranty text printed on the invoice or PO. Recovery runs in three passes, ordered from least to most disputed. Pass 1 is zero-dispute money: open and unapplied credit memos, duplicate payments, and core credits not applied. Pass 2 is the repeat-serial detector: the same S/N back to the same shop inside its window, plus the same S/N failing after different shops' repairs. Pass 3 is contested items: NFF fees on in-warranty units and turnaround-guarantee credits. Claims go out on each vendor's own form. A vendor playbook library covers the top 60 shops: warranty terms, exclusions, contacts, average days to credit and past acceptance rate. We chase every claim to a posted credit or cash. Phase 2 adds read-only receiving and removal data from the customer's ERP to confirm failures the invoices alone can't show.
mutants.why_now: Reliable, cheap LLM extraction from messy repair-invoice PDFs and warranty fine print is what makes an AP-only audit viable. Before 2025 it needed offshore data-entry teams, which killed contingency margins. Aftermarket parts prices and repair turn times have also climbed since the 2022-23 supply squeeze (my assumption, unverified). That makes each exchange unit worth more, so pools tie up more capital in them and each unclaimed failure costs more.
mutants.revenue_model: Contingency fee of 20% of cash and credits recovered, or 25% on contested pass-3 items, with a 12-month tail after the audit. The fee is due only when cash arrives or the credit is applied, not when the memo is issued. That solves the objection to paying cash on a credit the customer can only spend at that shop. There is no upfront cost and no minimum. Year 2 adds a $2-4k/month continuous-monitoring tier for pools with over $15M of spend. Anonymized vendor-acceptance and turn-time data is a later product.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Sequence matters more than segment. Leading with credits the vendor has already conceded gives first cash in 3-4 weeks, with no dispute and no relationship risk. That builds the trust to file contested claims later. Every contested claim, won or lost, adds to the playbook library: per-shop acceptance rates, exclusion language and time to credit. That library is the cornered resource and process power a generalist cannot copy. The pool is also the freight-audit shipper of aviation: high invoice volume, many vendors, serial-tracked goods and no reason to protect any single vendor.
mutants.first_30_days: Build a target list of about 60 pools and Part 145 stations from public repair-station and trade-association directories. Send 40 direct outreach messages offering a free scan: they send 12 months of vendor ledger and invoices, and we return the dollars found within 10 business days. The only thing we ask for is permission to file. Hire a retired warranty or materials coordinator as a paid advisor for vendor quirks. Close 3 audits and deliver ranked claim lists. File pass-1 claims first and aim for the first credit memo by day 30. Set an explicit kill test: if the median first-pass yield is under 1% of repair spend across the first 5 files, stop or narrow the segment. Publish the aggregate finding, such as the share of eligible repeat repairs never claimed, as the lead magnet.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Ramco's warranty module is software that large operators run themselves, and I could not verify its claims. This is an outsourced, success-fee claims service for smaller buyers, which Ramco does not offer. The Trax, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000 and CAMP homepages showed no claims features, though that is weak evidence. Generalist AP recovery-audit firms exist (an unresearched risk to check). They run duplicate-payment and vendor-statement logic and cannot read repair invoices, match serial numbers or judge warranty eligibility. Targeting pools and stations sidesteps PBH shielding, sidesteps the maintenance-system integration problem, and reduces relationship fear.

mutants.title: Warranty Desk Embedded in Maintenance Software
mutants.one_liner: A white-label, success-fee warranty desk sold through mid-tier maintenance-tracking and MRO software vendors. The removal event, the PO and the repair invoice meet inside a system the operator already uses, and the software vendor earns a revenue share.
mutants.customer: The channel buyer is the partnerships or customer-success head at a mid-tier maintenance-tracking or MRO software vendor with 50-400 operator customers. The payer is the operator on that software: a regional airline, Part 135 or cargo-feeder fleet, or helicopter operator. The vendor pays nothing. It receives 30% of our fee and gets a renewal and differentiation story.
mutants.problem: Operators on these systems already hold structured removal, install, hours and cycles data, plus POs and receiving records. That is the data-access problem the parent idea could not solve. Still, warranty stays unclaimed, because the missing pieces are things software does not do. Someone has to read negotiated PDF terms, file on each shop's own template, and chase the shop for 60-90 days. Vendors cannot staff claims specialists. Operators' thin materials teams cannot absorb the work. The claim is decided at the removal moment, when a technician pulls a unit at 3 AM and nobody sees the terms. Only the maintenance software sees that event.
mutants.solution: The vendor gives a read-only export or API for removals, installs, POs and receiving. We load each shop's warranty terms from the operator's contracts and invoice PDFs. When a technician posts a removal against a serialized component, we return a lookup card in seconds, inside the vendor's UI or by email or Slack in the first version. The card shows who repaired the unit and when, the remaining window in days, hours or cycles, the evidence checklist, and a pre-drafted claim. Our claims specialists then file, chase and post the credit memo back into the system as a warranty record. A monthly sweep catches misses, late turn times, no-fault-found fees and open cores. Operators sign a contingency agreement. The vendor contract is non-exclusive and revenue-share only.
mutants.why_now: LLM extraction of warranty fine print and invoice PDFs means one specialist can now run claims for dozens of operators. Software vendors are also under pressure to prove value in the renewals of small and mid-size operators. Ramco advertises warranty-recovery savings, which shows the outcome is being marketed. Nobody sells the outcome as a service to the other vendors.
mutants.revenue_model: Operators pay 20% of cash and credits recovered, with a 12-month tail. The vendor gets 30% of our fee, about 6 points of recoveries, and owns the relationship. From year 2, vendors can bundle a Warranty Desk line item at $1-2k/month per operator, with us as wholesale fulfillment at about $600/month plus the success fee. Aggregated vendor-level claim data is a later product.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Maintenance software has an adoption problem, not a feature problem. Warranty fields and modules sit empty because filling them takes human work: reading PDFs and chasing vendors. A managed service that makes the module produce cash is worth more to a vendor than building the feature. The vendor also supplies what our own sales cycle lacks: structured removal data, a warm introduction, and a trigger at the exact moment the claim is won or lost. Vendors will not build claim-chasing themselves. Terms are negotiated PDFs, and staffing claims desks is not a software margin.
mutants.first_30_days: Approach 8 mid-tier software vendors' partnership heads with a one-page offer: we make a slice of your customers' warranty tracking pay, with no cost to you and 30% of our fee. Ask each for 2-3 design-partner operators. Work as a concierge service, with no integration yet. The operator exports removals, POs and receiving from the software's standard CSV export, we match against invoice PDFs, and we deliver a ranked claim list with the vendor's customer-success manager on the call. Build the removal lookup as a simple web form or email responder. Sign a revenue-share MOU with the first vendor and aim for the first credit memo by day 30-45. Hire a retired materials coordinator for shop quirks. Success is 2 operators with live removal-time lookups by month 3.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Ramco is an ERP vendor with a warranty module for large operators. This does not compete with it as software. It targets vendors that lack a warranty offering, and Ramco or its implementation partners remain possible channels. Trax, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000 and CAMP homepages showed no claims features, so they are the intended partners. The offer differs from an ERP module because it is done-for-you and paid only on results. It avoids the data-access problem by using the vendor's structured data. It also avoids cold sales to small operators, since the vendor's existing customer base and success team provide distribution.

mutants.title: Chargeback Network for Aircraft Component Warranties
mutants.one_liner: A neutral claims network that moves a failed-repair claim up the chain from operator to pool to shop to piece-part supplier, inside each link's warranty window, with standard reason codes, response clocks and netted settlement. It starts as a back-to-back claim desk for rotable pools.
mutants.customer: The first customers are independent rotable pools and Part 145 stations that sell exchange units with warranty downstream and buy repairs with warranty upstream. They are the only parties who are both claimant and respondent. Shops and piece-part suppliers join as respondents, at no cost at first. Operators and lessors join as claimants. Airline procurement teams, lessors and insurers later buy shop-performance data.
mutants.problem: One rotable failure triggers a chain of warranties: operator to pool or lessor, pool to shop, shop to piece-part supplier. Each link has its own window, evidence rules, template and email address. The clocks are mismatched. A pool may give the operator a longer window than the shop gives the pool (a typical gap I have not verified). A claim arriving late in the downstream window is already dead upstream, and the pool absorbs the gap. Claims are rejected on paperwork, sent back and forth by email, and never passed up the chain in time. Nobody sees the whole chain. Every party recovers, or fails to recover, alone.
mutants.solution: Version 1 is a back-to-back desk for pools. It has an intake address and portal for customer claims. An LLM and rules engine check serial history, the warranty terms and the evidence. Valid claims are auto-converted into a standard upstream packet and sent to the pool's shop inside that shop's window. Invalid claims get a reason-coded response. The desk tracks each claim to a credit and sends a monthly netting statement of credits and debits with each counterparty, settling only the net. Shops receive a complete, pre-checked packet with one-click accept, deny or counter, response timers and a bounded dispute path. In parallel we publish open Rotable Claim Rules v1: reason codes (repeat failure, NFF in warranty, core, turn-time, piece-part defect), an evidence checklist, response clocks such as 10 days to acknowledge and 30 to decide, and a neutral technical panel for disputes. Later layers are shop scorecards for procurement, and advances on approved claims, an early cash payment against approved claims from a small credit facility.
mutants.why_now: Cheap LLM reading of repair paperwork, terms and evidence packs makes standard packets and pre-checks possible at low cost per claim. Higher unit values and longer repair turn times since the 2022-23 supply squeeze (my assumption, unverified) make each missed claim costlier and make pools hold more capital in exchange units.
mutants.revenue_model: Pools pay about $45 per claim processed plus 3% of upstream recoveries. Shops with more than 20 claims a month can pay $500-1,500/month for an adjudication assistant. Disputes cost about $250 per panel case. Year 2-3 adds shop-performance data subscriptions: repeat rate by P/N, days to credit, acceptance rate. Later, advances on approved claims at a small monthly discount, a balance-sheet layer priced from our own claim-outcome data.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The warranty chain is a chain of mismatched clocks and formats, and the intermediary pays for the gap. That intermediary is also the one participant who is both claimant and respondent, which is why a pool is the natural seed for a two-sided network, as issuers and acquirers are in card chargebacks. Standard reason codes and evidence rules make a claim cheaper to settle than to fight. Shops gain a filter for invalid claims. At scale the network holds the only serial-level record of repair durability across owners: lemon units, repeat-failure shops and days to credit. No single-company ERP can see that. Defensibility comes from network economies, switching costs in claim histories and netting, and the data.
mutants.first_30_days: Recruit 3 pools as design partners, using the free scan from the pool wedge as the way in. Point their customer-claim email address at a shared inbox we monitor. Process claims manually with LLM assistance for 30 days, and send upstream claims in the standard packet to 5 shops. Measure acceptance and days-to-credit against the pool's own baseline. Draft Rotable Claim Rules v0.1 with two retired shop warranty managers as advisors and circulate it to trade groups. Set the target as one upstream credit on a claim that would otherwise have missed its window. Then convert to paid pilots at $2-4k/month across 3-5 pools by month 6.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Ramco is a one-sided ERP module for large operators. This is a neutral layer between companies, which one company's ERP cannot be. The Trax, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000 and CAMP homepages showed no claims network. OEM warranty portals, as far as I know, run one way, from the OEM to its customers, and cover the OEM's own new-part warranty, not third-party repair warranties. That is a domain-knowledge assumption to check, as is whether ATA Spec 2000-type standards already cover warranty claims. The first product also needs no maintenance-system integration, and starts with a segment (pools) that has no PBH shield.
